A Caregiver’s hands. A Ruler’s order. A Hero’s nerve. A Sage’s clarity, so nobody dreads their numbers again.

A brand archetype report & differentiation strategy for Bayline Advisory Group · Bookkeeping, tax and accounting · St. Petersburg, FL
Brand Archetype Report Identity · Makeup · Questions for the call · Voice · Landscape · Differentiation · Visual Direction · November 2026
What this report is: the result of Bayline Advisory Group’s brand archetype assessment, scored with Skyway’s weighted engine across all twelve archetypes, then translated into identity, voice, a read of the market you’re working in, and the visual thinking that should carry it. And what it is not: a verdict. Your assessment returned four archetypes at exactly equal weight, so this report presents all four level, shows the tie in the open, and carries the twelve questions we’ll use on our call to settle the order between them.
01 · Brand Identity

The family firm that takes the case, keeps the books in order, and explains it in your language.

Your assessment did something rare: it refused to pick. Hero, Caregiver, Ruler and Sage each landed on 7 of 37, and nothing else came close. Read as a score, that is a tie. Read as a brand, it is a description. A firm that looks after people, keeps their affairs in order, takes on the fight when there is one, and explains the whole thing until the client understands it. The four are presented here at equal weight, because that is what you told us.

Caregiver · The Care
Nobody is a case number

Family owned, family run, and the motto you chose over eleven others: caring for others matters most. The relationship is the product everything else is wrapped in.

  • Your motto, “Caring for others matters most,” is the Caregiver’s, word for word.
  • “Approachable” is one of your three strengths; helplessness is among your deepest fears.
  • In your own words: “a family owned and operated business that cares about people.”
Ruler · The Order
Structure is the service

You chose the Executive, “authoritative and stable,” and a purpose “to provide structure for others.” Clean books, filed on time, a grant report the board can trust.

  • Your stated purpose: “to provide structure for others.” The Ruler’s, verbatim.
  • Your symbol is a key; your character is the Executive; “Confident” is a strength.
  • Fund accounting, grant reporting and IRS filings are structure, offered as a specialty.
Hero · The Nerve
The case other firms send away

IRS resolution is the work most accountants quietly refer out. You named it as the thing that could set you apart, and your answers about courage say why.

  • You reward people who “tackle challenges with courage and inspire others with their resilience.”
  • Your problem approach: “We confront obstacles head-on with courage.”
  • IRS resolution, which you call “dreadful for most people and organizations.” You walk toward it.
Sage · The Clarity
Understand your own numbers

The Owl, “intelligent,” a fear of misinformation, and a cozy reading nook. The outcome you want is a client who finally gets it, in whichever of three languages they think in.

  • You chose the Owl, the Sage’s ambassador, and “Intelligent” as a strength.
  • Among your fears: misinformation, the Sage’s fear word for word.
  • You speak English, Spanish and Portuguese: understanding, delivered in the client’s own language.

At the core, you’re four things at once, and the engine refused to rank them.

Most accounting firms score as a Caregiver with a Ruler behind it, and stop there: we look after you, we keep things tidy. Your answers kept adding to that. Courage showed up twice, in what you reward and in how you approach problems. Understanding showed up in the Owl, in “intelligent,” and in the fear of misinformation. Neither is decoration; each carries exactly as many points as the two drives the category takes for granted. Lean into: saying all four plainly, and never apologising for the two the category doesn’t expect.

Each one has a job.

The Caregiver is the relationship: the same person answers, nobody is made to feel stupid about a shoebox. The Ruler is the product: books that close, filings that go out early, a system the client can lean on. The Hero is the front door: the IRS letter nobody else wants to open, the case other firms refer out. The Sage is the outcome: a client who understands their own numbers and stops dreading them. Lean into: leading any one piece of communication with the drive that moment needs, and letting the other three show in the manner.

Why the combination is one-of-a-kind.

The twelve archetypes group into four families by core human drive, and your 37 points split Structural 16, Legacy 9, Spiritual 7, Connector 5. Structural (Caregiver, Ruler and a little Creator) is the centre of gravity: a firm whose instinct is to look after people by putting their affairs in order. What makes you unusual is the other two. The Hero comes from the Legacy family, the archetypes that leave a mark; the Sage from the Spiritual family, the ones that seek understanding. An accounting firm with equal parts care, order, nerve and clarity is not a type the category has a word for yet. That is the opportunity.

The one thing to make unmistakable
Plenty of firms will keep your books. Very few will open the IRS letter with you, fix it, and then teach you why it happened, in English, Spanish or Portuguese. Bayline is the family firm that does the hard part.
“Cared for. In order. Defended. Understood.”
The identity in four promises, at equal weight, in no particular order until you tell us otherwise
Two undertones sit underneath. Jester at 3 is the laugh on a client call that keeps a family firm human; it never leads, but it is why people stay. Everyman at 2 is “regular people, your language”: the trilingual welcome that makes a nervous first-time client pick up the phone. Both live in the manner, not the message.

The guardrail: four leads is one too many for any single sentence. A line that tries to be caring, authoritative, brave and wise at once will sound like a mission statement. Pick the drive the moment needs, say it plainly, and trust the other three to show in how it’s said.

For the review call · Twelve pairs

Both answers will be true. Pick the one you’d keep.

Each pair sets two of your four drives against each other in a scene from Bayline’s own world. Every option is something a good accounting firm would genuinely do; neither is the flattering one. You will want to say “both,” and both will be right. The question is always the same: if you could only keep one, which? Say the aside out loud. “Option two, but only if…” is usually the most useful thing in the session, and we write it down word for word.

A client arrives with three years of unfiled returns and an IRS letter they haven’t opened. What is the first thing Bayline says?

Option one

“You’ve been carrying this alone for long enough. From today, you don’t have to. Hand it to us and go sleep.”

Option two

“This is exactly the kind of case we take on, and the kind other firms quietly send away. We go at the IRS directly, and we get it resolved.”

A new business owner signs on, nervous and a little embarrassed about the state of their books. How does Bayline earn their trust in the first ninety days?

Option one

By explaining their own numbers to them, in plain language, in a way nobody has bothered to before. They leave the first meeting understanding where the money goes.

Option two

By showing them order: clean books by the end of month one, filed on time, a system that doesn’t wobble. They leave the first quarter knowing nothing will slip.

A non-profit director walks out of a meeting with Bayline. Which feeling do you most want them to have in the car?

Option one

Relieved. “Someone has this. I can stop worrying about the grant report.”

Option two

Clearer. “I finally understand how fund accounting works, and why the board keeps asking that question.”

A client needs a filing out by Friday. The books haven’t been reconciled, and reconciling properly takes until Monday. Which does Bayline do?

Option one

Hold the line. Nothing leaves the office until the books are clean. The client gets an extension filed and a straight explanation of why.

Option two

Take it on. The team works through the night, reconciles what matters, and makes Friday, because the client needed Friday and Bayline doesn’t leave people hanging.

A long-standing client sends receipts late, in a shoebox, every single quarter. What does Bayline do about it?

Option one

Put a system in place and hold them to it: a monthly cutoff, a portal, a process. That is what good care looks like, even when they grumble.

Option two

Absorb it. Build in the time, sort the shoebox, never once make them feel bad about it. They’re a client, not a project.

A non-profit’s board is panicking about an upcoming grant audit. Bayline is in the room. What is Bayline’s role?

Option one

The one who stands between the board and the auditor and handles it. The board’s job is to stop panicking; Bayline’s job is to win the audit.

Option two

The one who walks the board through exactly what the auditor will ask and why, so that this is the last audit they are ever frightened of.

A client asks a question you have already answered three times. Which is closer to what Bayline does?

Option one

Answer it once more, then build them a one-page explainer and a short video, because the real goal is that they stop needing to ask.

Option two

Answer it again, warmly, and as many times as it takes. That patience is part of what they are paying for.

Which sentence would you rather hear someone use to describe Bayline at a St. Pete chamber breakfast?

Option one

“They’re the firm that takes the cases nobody else will touch.”

Option two

“They run your finances so tightly that nothing ever gets to that point.”

A client wants to do something that is legal but, in Bayline’s judgement, unwise. What happens?

Option one

Bayline states its position and says it won’t prepare it that way. The client can take that advice or take their business elsewhere; the standard is the standard.

Option two

Bayline lays out exactly what happens under each path, in detail, and lets the client decide with the full picture in front of them.

Bayline’s single best review goes up online. Which one is it?

Option one

“They went to bat for us with the IRS and they won.”

Option two

“They treated us like family and never once made us feel stupid.”

A new client wants to work with Bayline but can’t afford the full package this year. What does Bayline do?

Option one

Find a way. A reduced scope, a payment plan, something, so that they are not left without help.

Option two

Keep the standard where it is and refer them to a firm that fits their budget. The service is the service, and it is worth what it costs.

The first line on Bayline’s new homepage. Which one?

Option one

“Finally understand your numbers.”

Option two

“Problems with the IRS? We resolve them.”

And one sentence to finish, in your own words. We’ll write down exactly what you say.

“People come to Bayline instead of a bigger firm because…”

It does not produce new points: the twelve scores above stay exactly as scored, the four stay level on points, and the order is recorded here as yours. 03 · Core Purpose

So nobody has to dread their numbers again

Bayline exists for the business owner who hasn’t opened the envelope, the non-profit director doing the fund accounting alone at eleven at night, and the family that has been filing in a second language for years and hoping it was right. It exists to take the dread out of money: by looking after the person, putting their affairs in order, taking on the IRS when the IRS has to be taken on, and explaining all of it until they understand it.

It’s the Caregiver’s purpose, to take the weight off, delivered the Ruler’s way, in order, with a Hero’s nerve for the hard cases and a Sage’s insistence that the client understands why.

Alternates to react to

We don’t just keep your books. We keep your peace of mind, and the books come with it.

The letter you’ve been afraid to open. Bring it here.

Accounting that explains itself. In English, Spanish or Portuguese.

04 · Voice & Personality

Speak like the family accountant who is actually in your corner.

If the brand were a person: a second-generation accountant in St. Pete who grew up in a house where two languages were spoken over the tax returns on the kitchen table. Calm in a way that calms other people. Exact without being fussy. Completely unbothered by an IRS letter, because she has read a thousand of them, and never once condescending to the person who was afraid to open it. Laughs easily. Hates jargon. Would rather you understood your balance sheet than admired hers.

Steady

We are organised, exact, on time  ·  not rigid, bureaucratic, or cold.
“Your books close on the fifth. Every month. That’s the whole point.”

Warm

We are present, patient, family  ·  not saccharine, soft on the facts, or pitying.
“You’re not in trouble with us. Bring the shoebox.”

Unflinching

We are direct, in your corner, willing to take the case  ·  not chest-thumping, or promising outcomes no one can promise.
“We’ll open the letter together. Then we go to work.”

Clear

We are plain-spoken, teaching, fluent in three languages  ·  not lecturing, academic, or hiding behind terms.
“Here’s what a restricted fund actually means for your grant report.”

On the dials: warm over polished · plain over technical · steady over urgent · direct over diplomatic · teaching over telling · family over firm · three languages, one voice.

Website blurb

“Bayline is a family accounting firm in St. Petersburg. We keep your books in order, we handle the IRS when it has to be handled, and we explain your numbers until they make sense, in English, Spanish or Portuguese.”

Email to a panicked client

“Got your message. Don’t open anything else from them; forward it to me. Here’s what happens next, in order, and none of it happens tonight.”

LinkedIn post

“Most non-profit directors didn’t get into this to learn fund accounting. Here’s the one thing about restricted funds that stops the board asking the same question every quarter.”

The guardrail: never promise an IRS outcome. The Hero’s nerve is in taking the case, not in guaranteeing the result; the category is full of firms that promise, and the IRS decides. “We take it on” is true. “We’ll get it settled for pennies” is the other camp’s line, and it is why people distrust them.
Part II · The Strategy

Now that we know who you are, here’s how you win.

Four drives at equal weight only matter if, together, they open a lane the competition can’t follow you into. So we mapped the market an online-only accounting firm actually competes in, and found three camps, each holding one of your four and none holding all of them.

05 · Competitive Landscape

Three camps. None of them own your lane.

You told us your reach is online only, with no geography, and you named no rivals. So the field is national, and it sorts into three camps a prospect would compare you against: the online bookkeeping platforms, the tax-resolution outfits, and the non-profit specialists. Each owns one of your four drives. None owns the combination. (Read from each brand’s public positioning on 2 November 2026 and to be validated with you on review; the camps are Skyway’s picks, since the brief named no competitors. A deeper teardown can follow.)

The online bookkeeping platforms

The open lane
One firm that is all three at once: the bookkeeper who’s there every month, the one who takes the IRS case, and the one who understands fund accounting, in three languages.

The platforms can’t be a family, the resolution outfits can’t be your bookkeeper, and the specialists can’t do your personal return. Each camp has built its brand around one of your drives. Nobody has built one around all four, because almost nobody has all four.

06 · Differentiation Strategy

Five ways to pull away

Each pillar targets the open lane, and each is something the brand should actively say, not just imply.

Say nobody gets a case number.

The platforms promise a “dedicated bookkeeper” and deliver a queue. The resolution outfits assign a case manager and a case ID. You are a family firm, and the same person picks up. That is the Caregiver, and in an online-only business it is the thing the big players structurally cannot copy.

In the brand Faces and first names on the site, not a stock photo of a team. Say who answers the phone. Stop writing “our team of experts”; write “you’ll talk to Michelle.”

Put the IRS letter on the front door.

Most firms bury IRS resolution three clicks deep, if they offer it at all. The only camp that leads with it is the resolution outfits, and they lead with debt minimums, free consultations and guarantees that the category is routinely warned about. You have no minimum, you don’t promise outcomes, and you’ll still be doing the client’s books next year. That is the Hero without the hype.

In the brand A dedicated page and one line on the homepage: “Problems with the IRS? Bring the letter.” Never a guarantee, never a dollar figure for what you’ll “save.”

Own fund accounting as a specialty, not a line item.

You told us you are passionate about philanthropy and have dedicated the firm to non-profit accounting: fund accounting, grant reporting, IRS filings. The non-profit specialists own that story nationally with mission language and scale claims. You can’t out-scale Jitasa; you can out-know a board. Speak to the director who has been doing it alone and the treasurer who dreads the 990.

In the brand A non-profit page written in the director’s language (restricted funds, grant reporting, the board question), with a Ruler’s calm and a Sage’s explanations. Case stories where the organisation finally understood its own numbers.

Lead in three languages, out loud.

English, Spanish and Portuguese. The platforms are English-only. Two resolution outfits advertise “bilingual,” meaning Spanish. Portuguese-speaking accounting is close to unique in a Tampa Bay market with a large Brazilian community, and online-only means the reach is national. This is the Sage’s understanding and the Everyman’s welcome in one move, and it is currently a clause at the end of a sentence in your brief.

In the brand A language toggle on the site, bios that state the languages, social templates built in all three. Say it on the homepage, not in the footer.

Sell order and understanding together.

The platforms deliver a dashboard. The specialists deliver a report. Neither guarantees the client understands it. Your Ruler puts the books in order; your Sage makes sure the client knows what the order means. Together they are the thing a client cannot get from software: a firm that explains itself.

In the brand Every monthly close goes out with three sentences in plain language on what changed and why. Make “finally understand your numbers” a promise you can point to.

Your strategic sweet spot
The family firm that does the hard part.

Cared for, in order, defended and understood, in whichever language you think in.

07 · Visual Identity · Concept Strategies

Three ways to look the part

Direction, not decoration: three strategic concepts for the brand’s visual identity, each true to the four drives and each weighted a little differently among them. We’ll design the chosen one once the call has settled the order.

Concept A
Quiet institution

The firm people trust with money, beautifully stated.

Navy ground, sand type, generous space, a classical high-contrast serif: the visual language of the institutions people trust with their finances. Leans Ruler and Sage.

Pros
  • Instantly credible with business owners and boards
  • Matches the luxurious, elegant, minimalist words you chose
  • A clean foil to the platforms’ app-store gloss
Tradeoffs
  • Needs real warmth from photography and voice or it reads as a bank
  • Underplays the family, the Caregiver’s strongest card
Concept B
Warm ledger

Order you can feel at home in.

Sand as the field, navy for type and structure, teal only as the accent. Ruled lines, paper textures, a serif with real weight. The order of a ledger and the warmth of a kitchen table. Leans Caregiver and Ruler, with room for both others.

Pros
  • Tells the family-firm story on sight
  • Ownable: nobody in any of the three camps looks like this
  • Holds all four drives without favouring one
Tradeoffs
  • Sand-heavy layouts need discipline to stay crisp on screens
  • Less overtly “digital” for an online-only firm
Concept C
Clear water

Approachable first, exact close behind.

Teal-forward, modern, light, with navy for weight and sand for warmth. Built for the online-only reality: clean screens, quick to read, friendly to a nervous first-time client. Leans Sage and Caregiver.

Pros
  • Lowest barrier for the client afraid of accountants
  • Extends naturally to social templates and a trilingual site
Tradeoffs
  • Drifts toward the bookkeeping-platform look you need to escape
  • Weakest at the Hero and the Ruler; can feel light for IRS work

The color thinking

You chose navy, sand and teal, and you ruled out rust, tangerine and stone. That is a coherent instinct: navy and sand are the Ruler’s and the “luxurious, elegant” words you picked; teal is the calm and clarity of the Sage and the Caregiver; and ruling out stone keeps the grey out that would kill the warmth. Two cautions. First, navy with sand-as-gold is the default of banks, wealth managers and law firms; keep the sand matte and warm, as paper rather than foil, or Bayline reads as somewhere you need an appointment. Second, navy with teal is the default of the bookkeeping platforms and the fintech apps behind them, so teal must stay an accent and never become the field, or the brand reads as software. In St. Pete specifically, navy beside a light blue drifts toward the Rays; keep the teal clearly green-leaning, never powder. The warmth lives in the sand, which is why Concept B uses it as the ground.

The type thinking

You chose “classical and high contrast,” which is right for the Ruler and the Sage: a serif with real authority for headlines, such as Fraunces or Playfair Display, paired with a humanist sans for everything a client has to read, such as Nunito Sans or Archivo. Two cautions. A high-contrast serif loses its hairlines at social-template sizes, so use the heavier optical size there or let the sans carry the small type. And an Owl plus a classical serif can tip into the old-bank register the Caregiver has to cut against; the humanist body face, generous spacing and the warm sand are what keep it a family firm. Set the three languages in the same two faces; both support Portuguese and Spanish diacritics properly.

Our lean: Concept B, executed with Concept A’s restraint. A warm, ordered system that carries all four drives without favouring one, until the call tells us which to favour.
08 · Summary

Four drives, level to the point. One firm that holds them all.

Care, order, nerve and clarity, at exactly equal weight, in a market where each camp has built a brand around one of them and nobody has built one around all four. The family firm that does the hard part. The order between the four is yours to set, and this report will carry it when you do.

Skyway Media · Visual direction

Colour, type and logo directions

Five palettes, five typefaces and five logo concepts for Bayline Advisory Group, built from the brand archetype report. Nothing here is a verdict; the review call decides.

For the review callNovember 2026
The brief · From the archetype report

Four archetypes at exactly equal weight. Every direction here leads with one of them.

Palettes, typefaces and logos are shown as three independent sets, so a direction can be built by mixing: one palette, one pairing, one mark.

Caregiver

The care

Family owned. Nobody is a case number. Warm, present, patient.

Ruler

The order

Structure is the service. The key. Organised, exact, confident.

Hero

The nerve

The IRS case other firms send away. Direct, unflinching, in your corner.

Sage

The clarity

Understand your own numbers, in English, Spanish or Portuguese.

Part one

Five colour palettes

Each leads with one of the four tied archetypes; the fifth holds all four level. Swatch notes name the role and where a colour fails contrast.

Palette 01 · Ruler-led · Order and trust

Harbor Ledger

Navy ink and brass: the key from the assessment, rendered as metal on paper. The firm whose books close on the fifth, every month.

Ink Navy#0F2742 · Primary, logo
Slate Blue#2F5A86 · Secondary, links
Brass#C9A24A · Accent, the key
Paper#F5F1E8 · Ground

BaylineAdvisory Group

Your books close on the fifth. Every month. That is the whole point.

Light ground, navy text, brass only on the one thing that matters.

Book a callOur services

Fit: Ruler first, Sage second. Brass is a highlight, never a fill behind body text; Mist is for lines, not type.

Palette 02 · Caregiver-led · Warm and present

Bayside

Deep teal water, sand, a little terracotta roof. St. Pete without a sunset filter. The family firm you bring the shoebox to.

Fit: Caregiver first, Everyman undertone. Terracotta is darkened so white text passes on it; keep it to buttons and one highlight per page.

Palette 03 · Hero-led · The case others send away

Near-black ink, bone paper, one stroke of vermilion. The envelope nobody wants to open, opened. Courage without alarm: the red is rationed.

Fit: Hero first, Ruler second. The red never carries body text or covers a page. It signals nerve, never a promised outcome.

Palette 04 · Sage-led · Understand your own numbers

Owl & Oak

Forest green, oak gold, parchment. The reading nook from the assessment and the Owl that came with it. The accountant who would rather you understood your balance sheet.

Oak Gold#B8862B · Accent, large type
Moss#6C7F5E · Secondary, badges

Fit: Sage first, Caregiver second. Oak gold fails contrast for small text, so it works as rules, numerals at 24px and up, and a lighter tint on dark panels.

Palette 05 · All four at level · Built for screens

Horizon

The bay at midday: navy, open blue, sky, a point of sun. The cleanest option for a website and Meta ads, and the one that does not tilt toward any single archetype.

Fit: balanced. Closest to the wider accounting category, so it leans on type and copy for distinctiveness. Sun takes navy text only, never white.

Part two

Five typefaces for the logo and brand

Every pairing is a Google Fonts family, free to install on every machine at the firm. Each specimen sets the wordmark, a headline from the report’s voice, and a line in English, Spanish and Portuguese.

Typeface 01 · Caregiver + Sage

Fraunces display  +  Inter body

Bayline
Advisory Group
Cared for. In order. Defended. Understood.
Your books close on the fifth. Every month. That is the whole point.
Sus libros se cierran el día cinco. Cada mes. De eso se trata.
Seus livros fecham no dia cinco. Todo mês. É esse o objetivo.

Why it fits. A soft, slightly old-style serif with real warmth in the curves. Reads as a family firm that has been here a while; the optical sizes keep it crisp on a tax notice.

Logo notes. Wordmark in Fraunces SemiBold at the 144 optical size, tracking −20. Descriptor in Inter SemiBold caps, tracking +260, about 60% of the wordmark’s width.

Typeface 02 · Ruler + Sage

DM Serif Display display  +  DM Sans body

Bayline
Advisory Group
Cared for. In order. Defended. Understood.
Your books close on the fifth. Every month. That is the whole point.
Sus libros se cierran el día cinco. Cada mes. De eso se trata.
Seus livros fecham no dia cinco. Todo mês. É esse o objetivo.

Why it fits. High-contrast, polished, a little formal. The closest of the five to established-firm credibility, the Ruler’s promise, with DM Sans keeping the body modern instead of stuffy.

Logo notes. One weight only, so the wordmark lives on spacing: tracking −10, tight line. Descriptor in DM Sans SemiBold caps. Best on the navy palettes (01, 05); thin serifs need a clean ground.

Typeface 03 · Hero + Ruler

Manrope display  +  Lora body

Bayline
Advisory Group
Cared for. In order. Defended. Understood.
Your books close on the fifth. Every month. That is the whole point.
Sus libros se cierran el día cinco. Cada mes. De eso se trata.
Seus livros fecham no dia cinco. Todo mês. É esse o objetivo.

Why it fits. The only sans-led direction. Manrope at ExtraBold is square-shouldered and direct, the Hero’s “we take it on” in letterform. Lora keeps the body warm so it never reads as a tech startup.

Logo notes. Wordmark in Manrope ExtraBold, tracking −35, sentence case. Holds a single-colour reverse on navy or vermilion. Best for signage, ad headlines and a square social avatar.

Typeface 04 · Sage, three languages

Source Serif 4 display  +  Source Sans 3 body

Bayline
Advisory Group
Cared for. In order. Defended. Understood.
Your books close on the fifth. Every month. That is the whole point.
Sus libros se cierran el día cinco. Cada mes. De eso se trata.
Seus livros fecham no dia cinco. Todo mês. É esse o objetivo.

Why it fits. A transitional serif built for long reading and a sans built to sit beside it. The most “explain it until you understand it” of the five, and both carry full Latin coverage, so Spanish and Portuguese accents set as cleanly as English.

Logo notes. Wordmark in Source Serif 4 SemiBold at the 60 optical size, tracking −15. Reliable in print, on letterhead and on IRS correspondence. Open licence.

Typeface 05 · Caregiver, with the Jester undertone

Bricolage Grotesque display  +  Newsreader body

Bayline
Advisory Group
Cared for. In order. Defended. Understood.
Your books close on the fifth. Every month. That is the whole point.
Sus libros se cierran el día cinco. Cada mes. De eso se trata.
Seus livros fecham no dia cinco. Todo mês. É esse o objetivo.

Why it fits. A grotesque with personality in the terminals: the laugh on a client call, made visible. Approachable without being cute, and Newsreader brings the Sage back into the paragraphs.

Logo notes. Wordmark in Bricolage Bold at the 96 optical size, tracking −30. The quirks show at large sizes only: the pick if the logo lives on signage, a website hero and social more than on engagement letters.

What the call decides

Three picks, one from each set. Mixing is allowed.

One palette

Harbor Ledger, Bayside, Open Letter, Owl & Oak or Horizon. Which archetype should the colour lead with?

One pairing

Serif-led (01, 02, 04), sans-led (03) or characterful (05). Where will the logo live most: letters or signage?

One mark

A B-mark (BL1 – BL3) travels across every palette; a sun mark (BL4, BL5) commits the brand to the bay.

Then Skyway delivers

The chosen mark as clean export files at the final hexes (full colour, one colour, reversed), the palette and type locked into a design system so every deck, ad and page pulls the same tokens, and the visual direction section of the archetype report updated to match.
